content: 1. Familial short stature is considered a normal variant of growth and does not require any specific treatment. Reassurance and regular monitoring of growth are sufficient. 2. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty also does not necessitate treatment in most cases. Reassurance and growth monitoring are recommended, with the potential option of sex steroid therapy during puberty if deemed necessary. 3. For small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants who exhibit catch-up growth, growth should be monitored to differentiate them from the 10% of SGA infants who do not experience catch-up growth. 4. In cases of undernutrition, reversing the nutritional deficit is essential to address growth failure caused by systemic disorders. 5. For patients undergoing glucocorticoid therapy, minimizing the glucocorticoid dose or administering it on alternate days, if feasible, is recommended. Alternative drugs should also be considered. 6. Gastrointestinal diseases, such as Crohn's disease and celiac disease, require diagnosis and treatment of the underlying condition, improvement of nutrition, and avoidance of glucocorticoids. 7. Rheumatologic diseases, particularly systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis, should be managed by diagnosing and treating the underlying disease, improving nutrition, and avoiding glucocorticoids. 8. Renal diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD) and renal tubular acidosis, require diagnosis and treatment of the underlying condition, optimization of nutrition, and growth hormone (GH) therapy if necessary. 9. In cancer patients, ensuring adequate nutrition and addressing any secondary pituitary hormone deficiencies, such as GH deficiency, is critical. 10. Pulmonary diseases, such as cystic fibrosis, immune deficiencies with recurrent pulmonary infections, or severe asthma, require diagnosis and treatment of the underlying condition, ensuring adequate nutrition, and avoiding glucocorticoids. 11. Immunologic diseases should be managed by diagnosing and treating the underlying condition. 12. Hypothyroidism as an endocrine cause of growth failure should be treated with thyroid hormone replacement therapy. 13. Cushing syndrome requires diagnosis and treatment of the underlying disease. 14. Growth hormone deficiency should be treated with recombinant growth hormone (rGH). 15. The treatment of precocious puberty depends on the specific type of the condition. 16. Genetic diseases with primary effects on growth, such as Turner syndrome, should be managed with estrogen and GH therapy. SHOX mutations, Noonan syndrome, and Silver-Russell syndrome may benefit from consideration of GH therapy. 17. Skeletal dysplasias, such as achondroplasia, require management of complications, which may include cranio-cervical junction compression, sleep apnea, and spinal stenosis. Hypochondroplasia necessitates surveillance for spinal stenosis, with surgery performed as needed. 18. Burn injuries are among the most devastating types of injuries, significantly impacting patients physically, physiologically, and psychologically. Burns remain a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. 19. Historically, treatments for burns were largely ineffective due to a lack of understanding of the pathophysiological impact of burns. However, advancements in biomedical research from the 18th to early 20th centuries, such as the recognition of burn surface area and skin grafting, laid the groundwork for modern burn care. 20. Despite these advancements, survival rates did not improve significantly until the past 50 years, when a better understanding of burn pathophysiology led to dramatic reductions in burn mortality. 21. Burn treatment is a complex process involving first aid, assessment of burn size and depth, fluid resuscitation, wound excision, grafting, infection control, and nutritional support. Progress in these areas has significantly enhanced survival rates for burn victims. 22. The history of burn care reveals that many advancements were driven by wartime experiences and fire disasters, such as the Rialto fire in 1921 and the Coconut Grove nightclub fire in 1942, which spurred research into the pathophysiology of burns. 23. Syringomyelia is a condition characterized by the formation of a cyst or tubular cavity, known as a syrinx, within the spinal cord. This syrinx can expand and elongate over time, causing destruction of the spinal cord. 24. Damage to the spinal cord in syringomyelia can result in pain, weakness, and stiffness in the back, shoulders, arms, or legs. Other symptoms may include headaches and a loss of the ability to sense extremes of hot or cold, particularly in the hands. 25. Syringomyelia can be caused by trauma, tumors, or congenital malformations such as hernias. It may lead to bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the upper extremities, as well as weakness, stiffness, and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, often accompanied by scoliosis. 26. The risk factors for syringomyelia depend on the underlying etiology, and the natural course of the disease is unpredictable. 27. Approximately 80% of patients with syringomyelia experience symptom resolution or improvement following surgical treatment. 28. Spinal MRI is a valuable tool for diagnosing and monitoring syringomyelia, often revealing characteristic findings. In some cases, syringomyelia may be incidentally diagnosed on CT scans or myelograms. 29. Chronic blepharitis should be managed with eyelid hygiene and topical antibiotics. If these measures are ineffective, oral tetracycline or doxycycline may be considered. 30. Inhalation injury in burn patients has been recognized as a significant cause of pulmonary complications since the 1970s. It has now surpassed burn shock and sepsis as the leading cause of mortality in burn patients. 31. Pulmonary complications from inhalation injury can result from direct damage to the respiratory tract due to inhalation of heated air and combustion chemicals, as well as iatrogenic factors such as fluid overload during resuscitation and mechanical ventilation-induced lung damage. 32. Smoke inhalation alone can cause airway and pulmonary inflammation, and inhalation injury is associated with pulmonary dysfunction lasting at least six months post-injury. 33. The global immunosuppression accompanying burn injuries increases the risk of respiratory tract infections, and treatments such as fluid resuscitation and blood transfusions can contribute to lung injury. 34. Mechanical ventilation using high tidal volumes can lead to excessive lung distension, disruption of pulmonary epithelium and endothelium, and release of inflammatory mediators. Lower tidal volume ventilation has been shown to reduce mortality and pulmonary complications in patients with acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome. 35. Most burn centers now adopt low tidal volume ventilation to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury. 36. Minor burns should be treated by cooling the burn with cool (not cold) water, removing tight items before swelling occurs, avoiding the breaking of blisters, applying lotion to prevent drying, bandaging the burn to reduce pain and protect the skin, and taking over-the-counter pain relievers. A tetanus shot should be considered if not up to date. 37. Surgical procedures for burns may include breathing assistance, nutritional support via feeding tubes, escharotomy to relieve pressure, skin grafts, and plastic surgery to improve scar appearance and joint flexibility.
